drills.coachNote: Look at your bishop on d4 - it looks defended by your rook on a4 along the fourth rank, but White's own pawn on b4 sits right between them, so that defense is an illusion. When you play Qe6 offering the trade, White grabs it with Qxe6, you recapture Rxe6, and now Rd1xd4 just wins your bishop clean because nothing was actually guarding it. That one overlooked pawn on b4 cost you a full piece and flipped a game you were doing fine in into a loss. Instead c5 keeps the tension, and after Bd5 cxb4 axb4 Rxa2 Bxa2 you trade down with your material intact - always check whether a defender's line is truly open before allowing a trade.

drills.title: vs Bodda_74 (684) — Italian Game
drills.coachNote: Notice your knight on g4 - it's sitting there completely undefended, and White's queen on g3 is eyeing it right down the g-file. You play Bb5, ignoring it, and Qxg4+ just wins the knight with check, kicking your king to f8 before White consolidates with Qh5. That's a full piece for nothing, swinging a position where you were clearly better into one where White's on top. The fix is h5 first, defending g4 with the pawn, so if White ever trades on g4 you recapture hxg4 and keep the piece, then push f5 hitting the bishop on e4. Always ask 'is this piece defended' before spending a move on something else.

drills.coachNote: You're completely winning here, up a huge chunk of material in this queen ending, and the only thing that can save White is checks against your king. Playing g6 does nothing for that plan but opens new light-square holes in front of your own king, and White pounces with Qc4+, forcing Kh7, then g4 gains space while Qe5 offers a trade that lets White's king catch up. That single pawn move nearly threw away a completely winning game. Instead Qb5 keeps your queen active and away from checks, and after Kg2 Kf8 Kf2 Qd7 Qc4 you calmly walk your king to safety first - in queen endings, don't touch a pawn near your own king unless it removes a check, not invites one.

drills.coachNote: Before you jump the knight to e4, scan White's queen on c5 for a check first - it has Qf5+, and that's exactly what happens. Your king gets shoved to h8, and then Qxe4 simply scoops up the knight you just placed, since nothing was covering e4. That one move turned a position where you were clearly ahead into one where White's better. Always look for the opponent's checks before committing a piece to a new square - a check can deflect your king and win material the very next move. drills.coachNote: Your knight on g5 is your most awkward piece right now, and instead of activating it you shuffle the king with Kf3, which does nothing for the position. Black's rook on c4 just grabs the pawn on b4 for free with Rxb4, since nothing was defending it, and after Ke2 Ra4 e4 you're worse off with no compensation to show for the lost pawn. The point isn't that b4 was savable - even in the best line it eventually falls - it's that you should get value for it. Nf3 followed by Nd4 plants your knight on a monster central outpost, and after Bd7 Nd4 g5 fxg5 you're active enough that losing b4 barely matters. Activate your worst piece instead of drifting with the king when a pawn's going anyway.

drills.coachNote: Your rook on c2 was the only thing holding your pawn on c3, and when you play Rd2 you walk away from that job. drills.title: vs NguyenTuanHai555 (860) — Vienna Game Anderssen Defense
drills.coachNote: Your king on g6 is already trapped in a mating net, and Bxf7 has been mate on the board this whole time - the bishop on c4 slices in, your own knight on g5 covers the king's only recapture on f7, your pawn on e4 seals off f5, and the queen on h4 rakes the whole h-file so h5, h6 and h7 are all covered, with your pawn on g7 and knight on f6 blocking what's left. Playing Rh8 does nothing about that, and Bxf7 ends the game on the spot. Nh5 was the real try - moving the knight off f6 opens an escape square there, so after Bxf7+ your king slides to f6 instead of getting mated, and play continues with Qxg4 Qxg5 Qxg5+ Kxg5. When your king has wandered this far forward, checking for an immediate mate comes before everything else.

drills.coachNote: Your bishop on g4 hits the queen on f3, but White just sidesteps to g3, and from there the queen quietly eyes your kingside where you've already loosened things with ...h6. Nothing gets won on the spot - c6 and Kh1 and b5 follow and White's still comfortable - but you've spent a move harassing a queen that didn't mind moving while your knight on b8 sits undeveloped. Nc6 keeps your development on schedule, and if White still plays Qg3, your knight jumps to h5 hitting the queen again with real tempo, with lines like Qg6 Qh4 Bxh6 showing your pieces working together on the dark squares. Chase a piece only when the chase itself accomplishes something - here just finishing development did more.

drills.coachNote: Black's queen on g2 is deep in your camp, but chasing her with Rg1 doesn't trap anything — g2 to h3 is wide open, and there's a pawn sitting there for the taking. She just slides to h3, grabs it, and after Nbd2 Ne7 she's already swinging around to Qa4+ for another check. When an enemy queen strays deep into your position, look for a square that both attacks her and wins material if she takes the bait — not just any square that seems threatening.

drills.title: vs Dantempo06 (865) — Queens Pawn Opening Accelerated London System
drills.coachNote: You were completely winning here, and the real edge wasn't material — it was black's king stuck on e7, unable to castle. Qg5+ invites a queen trade: Qxg5, Nxg5, and once the queens are off, black's knight jumps into e5 and the rook swings to d1, and a chunk of your advantage disappears with the queens. Qf4 keeps them on the board and keeps hunting that king — black answers Qd6, and even if you check again with Qg5+, he just meets it with Qf6, no trade, after which Qxd5 nets you the pawn anyway with the attack still alive. When your opponent's king can't castle, that's worth more than any single pawn — don't rush to simplify away the hunt.

drills.title: vs Mohamed_Behery (840) — Queens Pawn Opening Horwitz Defense
drills.coachNote: Your knight on f3 has a check waiting on d5 that forks the king on e7 and the queen on c7 at once — that's the shot to spot before grabbing material. Nxh7 wins a pawn, but it pulls your best piece off its dominant post on f6, and black regroups with Rd8; even after Qf6+ Ke8 the king just slips to safety and you're left picking up scraps with gxf4. Nd5+ keeps the hammer swinging: after exd5, Rfe1+ forces the king to d6, and Qxf8+ wins the rook outright while the king's still running. A fork with check almost always beats a free pawn, because check strips away your opponent's time to consolidate.

drills.title: vs edekyihotmailcom (766) — Queens Pawn Opening
drills.coachNote: You had mate in two sitting on the board and grabbed a pawn instead. Nf4+ forces Ke3 — it's forced, since your knight covers every other square around him — and then Bc5# finishes it, your bishop on d5 delivering mate with the king boxed in on e3. Qxe5+ also checks and nets a pawn, but the king just steps aside, and after Ne4, Bxe4, Qc1, O-O-O, white actually gets to trade pieces and tuck his king away instead of getting mated. You were up so much material either way that it didn't cost the win, but it's the habit to fix — when a check comes with a forcing follow-up that traps the king completely, look one move further before cashing in.

drills.title: vs edekyihotmailcom (766) — Queens Pawn Opening
drills.coachNote: White's king is still stuck on e1, and every check you give him is gold because he's got nowhere safe to run. Qg3+ forces Ke2 immediately, and then Qxe5+ grabs a pawn with another check — after Kf2 Qd4+ Ke2 you're shuffling his king around while helping yourself to material the whole way. Ne6 instead lets him play the quiet Qc1, getting his queen to a useful defensive square; you still eventually grab the e5 pawn with check, but now he's got time to block with Ne2 before you can pin things down with Bb4. When the enemy king hasn't castled, reach for the check first — it costs him tempo he can't spare.

drills.explanation: Both your queen and rook could capture the knight on f4, but Qxf4 is the right way: it wins the knight while the rook on f8 keeps guarding its partner on e8. Rxf4 abandoned that rook — Qxe8+ snapped it off with check, and after Kh7, Qe6 left White completely consolidated. Taking with the wrong piece cost about six pawns.
drills.title: vs prusten63 (873) — Italian Game
drills.coachNote: You've got two rooks on the back rank, e8 and f8, and Rxf4 pulls the f8 rook away — but that rook was part of what kept e8 safe. The instant White plays it, Qxe8+ crashes in, the queen on h5 swooping down the h5-e8 diagonal to grab your rook with check, and your position collapses from roughly equal to losing. Qxf4 was right there instead — your queen on g5 takes the knight just as well, keeps both rooks connected on the back rank, and after Qe2 e3 you're still fine. Before you grab a piece, always check what was defending what before it moves.

drills.explanation: a6 strikes at White's overextended queenside: after bxa6 Rxa6 your rook enters the game down the a-file, and b5 is met calmly by Ra8. Castling let White play Qe2, hitting your knight on c4 — a piece with no defenders — and you had to scramble with c6 and b5 just to hold it, leaving White a wedge pawn on c6.
drills.title: vs prusten63 (873) — Italian Game
drills.coachNote: The real story on move 12 is the pawn on b5 — that's the lever you needed with a6 right now, hitting it and threatening to rip open the a-file for your rook. Castling isn't wrong on its own, but it lets White play Qe2 and consolidate, and after c6 bxc6 b5 White gets that pawn wedge on b5 locked in for good, cramping your whole queenside and leaving your knight on c4 and bishop on e7 short on scope. It's not that O-O drops material, it just lets White fix the structure exactly how he wants — when a pawn lever is sitting there, take it first.

drills.explanation: You were a full piece up and just needed to consolidate. c5 gains space, and the knight calmly reroutes to c6 next with b6 and normal development to follow. Ng4 put the knight on a square covered by White's queen all the way back on d1 — Qxg4 took it for nothing, handing the extra piece straight back.
drills.opening: Caro Kann Defense Two Knights Attack
drills.title: vs Feri206 (798) — Caro Kann Defense Two Knights Attack
drills.coachNote: Your knight jumps from e5 to g4, but stop and ask what it's actually doing there — it isn't defended by anything, and it isn't threatening anything serious either, since f2 is guarded by White's rook on f1. White simply plays Qxg4 and you've dropped a full piece for nothing. That's the lesson: before you move a piece to a square, check who's covering that square, not just what it attacks. c5 was the move instead — grabbing central space and preparing ...Nc6, developing with a purpose rather than hanging a knight in the middle of the board.

drills.explanation: Bxa2 trades off White's light-squared bishop on your terms: after Rxa2 you swing rooks to the e-file with Rae8 and Re6, sitting solidly behind the e5 pawn. Rad8 left the bishops eyeballing each other one move too long — Bh6 came with threats at your king, and after g6, Bxe6 fxe6 left you with doubled, weak e-pawns.
drills.opening: Caro Kann Defense Two Knights Attack
drills.title: vs Feri206 (798) — Caro Kann Defense Two Knights Attack
drills.coachNote: You're already down a lot here, but Rad8 is a passive move that lets White dictate the play. White plays Bh6, hitting your rook on f8 and forcing g6 to stop the threat — permanently weakening the dark squares around your king — and then the bishop on a2 slides down its own diagonal to take your good bishop on e6, fxe6 leaving you with a worse pawn structure. Bxa2 was the move instead: it simply trades your bishop for White's on a2, and after Rxa2 you play Rae8, activating your rook on the only file where you still have counterplay. Even in a bad position, look for your own active resource instead of just developing quietly.

drills.explanation: Nxc6 wins a full rook: the knight captures its counterpart and forks the queen on e7 and the rook on d8, so after Qd6 saves the queen, Nxd8 collects the rook and Qxg5 even adds a pawn. a4 instead gave Black time for Nxe5, trading off your monster knight, and after Qxe5 his other knight landed on e4 with real counterplay.
drills.opening: Queens Pawn Opening Accelerated London System
drills.title: vs TheArtifier (833) — Queens Pawn Opening Accelerated London System
drills.coachNote: You had a hammer here: Nxc6 knocks out Black's defender first, and after Qd6 your other knight jumps in with Nxd8, forking the rook and winning the exchange clean — after Qxd8, Qxg5 grabs another pawn while eyeing the open g-file. Instead a4 is a slow pawn push that hands Black the initiative: Nxe5 trades off your attacking knight, and after Qxe5 the other knight lands on e4, forking your undefended c3 pawn and f2 near your king. You're forced into f3 just to kick it out, and your +4.8 crashes to barely +1. Spot a forcing combination like Nxc6-Nxd8 and play it immediately — a quiet pawn move only gives the opponent time to defuse it.

drills.explanation: Nxc6 is a fork: from c6 the knight hits both the queen on e7 and the rook on d8, so bxc6 is forced — wrecking the pawn cover in front of the king on c8. Then Qd3 turns on the knight on e4, and after Nxc5 bxc5 you're clearly on top. b5 abandoned the b4 pawn's guard of your c5 knight, and Nxe5 won material — no recapture worked.
drills.opening: Queens Pawn Opening Accelerated London System
drills.title: vs TheArtifier (833) — Queens Pawn Opening Accelerated London System
drills.coachNote: Your knight on e5 is actually hanging — your queen on e3 looks like it guards that square, but the e-file is blocked by Black's own knight on e4. So when you pushed b5 to hit the c6 knight, Black ignored the threat and just played Nxe5, scooping your loose knight for free; after bxa6 bxa6 your other knight even has to hop to b3 just to dodge the e4 knight. That's a whole piece gone — from +1.2 to nearly lost. The fix was Nxc6 immediately: take the attacked knight yourself before Black can redirect, and after bxc6 Qd3 you're a clean piece up while still hitting e4. Check what's loose on your own side before you go attacking.

drills.explanation: Rxf7 forces mate in three: your queen on d5 X-rays g8 so f7 can't really be held, and after Rg7+ Kh8, Rg8 is checkmate — the bishop on f6 seals g7 while the queen on d5 guards g8, so the rook can't be taken. Qg5 instead let Black play Rxf2 and keep the counterplay alive.
drills.title: vs yassine3453 (860) — Englund Gambit
drills.coachNote: You had a forced mate sitting right there and walked past it. Rxf7 rips away Black's last defender, and with your bishop on f6 locking down the dark squares, the rook swings to g7 with check, the king's forced to h8, and Rg8 is mate. Instead you played Qg5, a slow regroup that let Black's rook on c2 crash in with Rxf2, and suddenly Qe5 and Rf3 are biting into your own king safety — the mate vanished and you handed him real counterplay. When your opponent's king is this boxed in, look for the move that rips the position open, not the quiet regroup.

drills.explanation: Qxc8 wins the rook on c8 outright — Black never dares recapture, since your bishop on f6 and rook on e7 strangle his king; he tries Qb5, and after Re8 he must throw his queen away with Qf1+ Rxf1. Qd5 let a won game slip: Qxa3, and after Qxd4, Qxh3 stripped your king — nearly fifteen pawns of advantage gone.
drills.title: vs yassine3453 (860) — Englund Gambit
drills.coachNote: There's a rook just sitting on c8 with nothing covering it — not the f8 rook, not the king — so Qxc8 wins it outright on top of a position that's already crushing. Instead you played Qd5, centralizing but leaving that rook alone, and it let Black's queen on b2 go to work: Qxa3 grabs a pawn, then Qxh3 comes with check, and you're stuck babysitting your king with R7e3 while the win evaporates. When you're this far ahead, scan for hanging material before you reach for the 'nice' square — Qxc8 was simply free, and Qb5 next keeps squeezing toward an easy win.

drills.explanation: The g5 pawn was attacking your bishop on f4, and Nxg5 meets that head-on — the knight is covered by that same bishop, and after fxg5 Bxg5 Black's kingside pawns are stripped while his pieces retreat to passive squares like Nf6 and Nb8 as Qf3 builds pressure. Bf5+ dropped a whole piece instead: e6 blocked the check and hit the bishop, and after Bc2, gxf4 won your dark-squared bishop.
drills.opening: Queens Pawn Opening Accelerated London System
drills.title: vs jatin221272 (817) — Queens Pawn Opening Accelerated London System
drills.coachNote: This is the same picture as a couple moves ago — your bishop on f4 is hanging to the pawn on g5, and Bf5+ with the other bishop doesn't fix that. Black just answers e6, gaining a tempo by attacking your bishop, you're forced back to the miserable c2 square, and then gxf4 simply collects the piece you never protected. Since that bishop is falling no matter what, the stronger idea is Nxg5 — sac the knight to blow open the black king, still stuck on d7. After fxg5 Bxg5 you're hitting f6, and after Nf6 Qf3 you're piling pressure on b7 and the king, real compensation instead of losing material for a hollow check.

drills.explanation: Nxg5 was the shot: after fxg5 Bxg5 you get two pawns for the knight and Black's king on d7 is stranded, with Qf3 coming to hit the loose d5 pawn (the simple e4 was strong too). Bf5+ backfired — e6 blocked with tempo, the bishop crawled back to c2, and gxf4 scooped up your dark-squared bishop, which the g5 pawn had been eyeing all along.
drills.opening: Queens Pawn Opening Accelerated London System
drills.title: vs jatin221272 (817) — Queens Pawn Opening Accelerated London System
drills.coachNote: Notice Black's pawn on g5 is already attacking your bishop on f4 — that piece is going no matter what you play here. Bf5+ with the other bishop doesn't save it and doesn't achieve anything: Black blocks with e6, gaining a tempo, you're pushed to the passive c2 square, and gxf4 takes the piece anyway, so you paid for nothing. Since it's lost either way, the point is to get value for it — e4 strikes the center immediately, and even after gxf4 you answer exd5, grabbing d5 and following with Qa4+ to pick up more since Black's king is stuck in the middle. Make the piece you're losing buy you something.

drills.explanation: Your knight on e4 was attacked by the d3 pawn, and Nd6 is the safe retreat — White wins the e5 pawn with Rxe5+, but Be7 blocks, Bg6 follows, and you're only down a pawn with pieces coming out. Ng5 ran the knight straight onto the c1-bishop's diagonal: Bxg5 won it outright, and White grabbed e5 with the knight as well.
drills.title: vs Stwilso1 (836) — Ruy Lopez Opening Berlin Defense
drills.coachNote: Your knight lands on g5 and nothing defends it — not the bishop on f5, not the f7 pawn — and White's bishop on c1 sits right on the c1-to-g5 diagonal, so Bxg5 just wins it clean. That's the whole story of the 5-pawn swing: one hanging piece. The safer square was Nd6, tucking the knight back while covering f5 and f7; White can still grab a pawn with Rxe5+ since your king's stuck on e8, but after Be7 and Qe2 you're only down a pawn in a solid position, not down a full piece. Before sending a knight forward, ask what's actually defending the square it's landing on — g5 had nothing.

drills.explanation: Your knight on g5 was attacked by the bishop on c1, defended only by your queen along the d8–g5 diagonal — and Be7 blocked that exact diagonal. Bxg5 won the knight, and after Be6, Bxe7 Qxe7 left White a clean piece up. Ne6 just steps to safety; after Qf3 Qf6 Nxc6 Bxd3 the position stays a fair fight.
drills.title: vs Stwilso1 (836) — Ruy Lopez Opening Berlin Defense
drills.coachNote: That knight on g5 is still hanging — same bishop on c1, same diagonal, and Be7 does nothing about it. White plays Bxg5 again, and this time trades it for your other bishop too with Bxe7 Qxe7, so you're down a full knight for nothing, two moves running now. The move was Ne6, finally pulling that knight to safety instead of ignoring it — after Qf3 Qf6 Nxc6 Bxd3 you're trading into a real fight instead of a piece down. Once a piece has been hanging for a move already, fixing it has to jump to the top of your list before anything else on the board.

drills.explanation: Bc7 hits the queen on d8 and grabs a square deep in Black's camp: after Qd7, b6 locks the bishop on c7 permanently, cramping the whole queenside while Ra4 swings the rook toward the action. Your e4 gave Black a free move for Bd7, developing with a hit on the b5 pawn — the same Bc7 idea then came a tempo late, and the queen slipped away to c8.
drills.title: vs slammerman001 (850) — Indian Game
drills.coachNote: Right now your bishop on f4 has a shot at the queen — Bc7 hits d8 directly, and because Black's own bishop is still stuck on c8 with nothing to interpose, the only answer is the awkward Qd7, after which b6 and Nc6 keep squeezing the queenside. You played e4 instead, a fine move in a vacuum, but it hands Black a free tempo to play Bd7 first, so by the time you finally get to Bc7 the queen just tucks back to c8 already covered and Black's lost nothing. When a piece is attackable right now, ask whether waiting lets your opponent patch the problem before you cash it in.

drills.explanation: Qc5 does three jobs: it confronts the queen on b6, attacks the knight on e7, and keeps the b5 pawn defended. After Qd8, Bd6 piles onto e7, and Bxe7 Rxe7 leaves you in full control of the dark squares. Qc3 left b5 with no defender at all — Bd7 came immediately, and after your too-late Qc5, Bxb5 took the pawn for free.
drills.title: vs slammerman001 (850) — Indian Game
drills.coachNote: On c5 your queen forces the issue - it eyes Black's queen on b6 for a trade and threatens Bd6, hitting the rook on f8. Qc3 backs off that pressure, and now the b5 pawn, which nothing was actually guarding, becomes a target: Black plays Bd7, then after Qc5 Bxb5 you're down a clean pawn with your queenside sagging. Look at what Qc5 delivers instead - if Black dodges with Qd8, you play Bd6 hitting f8, force Re8, then Bxe7 nets the knight. The habit to build: before you shuffle your queen to a quiet square, check every pawn it was covering.

drills.explanation: Nf5+ is a fork: it checks the king on g3 and attacks the rook on g7 at the same time. After Kf4 you play Nxg7, winning the rook and flipping the game — roughly twelve pawns of swing. Nb7 instead walked into Rc7+, and after Kd8 the rook simply captured the knight on b7.
drills.opening: Queens Pawn Opening Zukertort Chigorin Variation
drills.title: vs OdisseoAP (826) — Queens Pawn Opening Zukertort Chigorin Variation
drills.coachNote: You were already crushing here, but the real shot was Nf5+ - check on the king stuck on g3, and after Kf4, Nxg7 simply grabs White's rook for free. Instead Nb7 walks into Rc7+: the rook swings to c7 with check, your king gets shoved to d8, and the knight on b7 - now completely undefended - falls to Rxb7. That's a piece lost for nothing in a position you should've been winning outright. Notice the pattern: Nf5+ does two jobs in one move, kicking the king away AND opening the road to the rook on g7 - always look for checks that double as setups.

drills.explanation: Bxg3+ wins a pawn with check, and after the forced Kxg3, Rxd1 scoops the rook — d1 had no defender at all, so you net rook and pawn for the bishop. Rd7 put your rook on a square nothing defends (the knight on c6 doesn't cover d7): Rxd7 took it for free, and after Bd6, bxc6 grabbed your knight as well.
drills.opening: Queens Pawn Opening Zukertort Chigorin Variation
drills.title: vs OdisseoAP (826) — Queens Pawn Opening Zukertort Chigorin Variation
drills.coachNote: Your rook on d8 already stared down White's rook on d1 along the open d-file, so sliding to d7 just hands it over - Rxd7 wins it clean since nothing was covering that square. It even snowballs: after Bd6, bxc6 grabs your knight too, and you're down a rook and a knight for one pawn. Compare that to Bxg3+: the bishop grabs the pawn on g3 with check, forcing Kxg3, and only then does Rxd1 work, because the king has just been dragged away from its own rook on d1. Same idea, opposite outcome - find the check that wins material first, instead of just sliding a piece into an open file.

drills.explanation: Qxb7+ forces checkmate: the queen grabs b7 and checks the king on e7 along the wide-open seventh rank, Black must block with Qc7, and Qxc7 is mate — your knight on f6 covers the escape squares e8 and d7, and the e5 pawn guards the knight. exd4 was a pawn grab with mate on the board; after Bg7 Black started breathing again.
drills.opening: Queens Pawn Opening Accelerated London System
drills.title: vs pisitto999 (814) — Queens Pawn Opening Accelerated London System
drills.coachNote: Black's king on e7 sits on a seventh rank that's completely open on c7 and d7, and your queen on f3 can swing straight down it. Qxb7+ does exactly that - check along the rank, Black's only real answer is Qc7 blocking with the queen, and then Qxc7 is mate, since your knight on f6 and pawn on e5 cover every escape square. Instead exd4 just recaptured a pawn and let that mate slip away; you were still winning afterward, but a forced mate in two became a long grind. When the enemy king's rank or file is that exposed, hunt for the check before reaching for the free pawn.

drills.explanation: Rd7+ is a deflection: the queen on c7 has to capture, and Nxd7 then forks the rook on b8 and the bishop on f8 — you've won queen for rook, with Rd1 coming to support the knight. Nd7 tried the fork without the preparation: Bg7 simply stepped the bishop out, nothing was won, and Rd6 got met by Rbc8. The open d-file was the key — use it with check first.
drills.opening: Queens Pawn Opening Accelerated London System
drills.title: vs pisitto999 (814) — Queens Pawn Opening Accelerated London System
drills.coachNote: You had a check that wins material outright: Rd7+ forces Qxd7 - Black's queen is the only piece that can deal with it - and then Nxd7, your knight from f6, scoops up the queen that just landed there, netting a queen for a rook. Instead you played the knight straight to d7 without the check, forking the rook on b8 and bishop on f8, but Black just saves the bigger piece with Bg7 and you win far less. The takeaway: when a check deflects the enemy queen onto a square your other piece already covers, play the check first - a forced capture beats a fork the opponent gets to choose from.

drills.explanation: Your queen on a4 was attacked by the knight on c5 and had to reach safety first — Qa3 does it. The Qh4 attacking idea was right but needed f6 first: after f6 gxf6, Black's own pawn on f6 blocks the e7–h4 diagonal, and only then is Qh4 strong. Played immediately, Qh4 landed right on the e7-queen's diagonal — Qxh4 won your queen on the spot.
drills.title: vs Iamastalemate (860) — Indian Game
drills.coachNote: Black's queen on e7 has a completely clear diagonal running through f6 and g5 straight to h4 - both squares are empty - so any piece you drop on h4 is simply hanging. That's exactly what Qh4 does: Black just plays Qxh4 and you've handed away your queen for nothing in a position you were already struggling in. Qa3 keeps the queen off that diagonal entirely and lets you just get on with the game - Re8, c4, d4, g4, normal maneuvering, no fireworks needed. Before you land a piece on any square, trace the diagonals and files already pointed at it; e7-h4 was wide open and it cost you the game.
